tagline: A winding paved road through Rogue River canyons and forested slopes
intro: The Galice-Hellgate Back Country Byway follows a narrow, winding paved road, with single-lane sections and occasional turnouts. The Bureau of Land Management presents Rogue River country as its central attraction: canyon rock walls, forested slopes and places to reach the river. One stretch climbs away from the river into the Siskiyou Mountains, with views of mountains and Douglas fir. Allow one to two hours to visit the byway, with pullouts and developed recreation sites along the route.

Galice began as a mining community in 1852, first occupying Galice Creek rather than its present site on the Rogue. Logging displaced mining in the mid-20th century, then gave way to tourism. The trail reached at Grave Creek has a separate history: the Takelma Indians developed it, and miners and settlers later improved it as they moved deeper into the canyon. At Rand, Civilian Conservation Corps workers built roads and trails and developed campgrounds in the surrounding national forest after a camp opened there in 1933.

Begin at the Merlin exit from I-5 and travel west on Merlin-Galice Road through Merlin. Continue through Galice to the former ranger station at Rand, now home to the Smullin Visitor Center. At Grave Creek, the byway provides access to the Rogue River National Recreation Trail.
notice: Canyon rock walls rise beside forested slopes along much of the drive.

moments.title: Merlin
moments.text: Merlin began its railroad story under another name. The station established here in 1883 was called Jump Off Joe, after a local stream. In October 1886 it became Merlin, a name chosen by a railroad civil engineer for the falcons he saw here. The post office moved to the station vicinity and took the same name in 1891. The community sits in the Jumpoff Joe Creek valley, four miles east of its meeting with the Rogue, in an area known for fishing and whitewater rafting. On the byway, Merlin comes four miles after the I-5 exit.

moments.title: Galice
moments.text: The original Galiceburg stood upstream on Galice Creek; Galice now occupies the Rogue River below the creek junction. The post office also moved downriver in 1922, before closing entirely in 1927. Settled as a mining community in 1852, it took its name from founder Louis Galice. Gold prospecting made the creek busy in the 1850s, but mining did not remain the principal industry. Logging took that role in the mid-20th century, followed by tourism. Nearby Hellgate Canyon became a filming location for parts of the 1975 John Wayne film Rooster Cogburn.

moments.title: Rand Ranger Station
moments.text: Before Rand had a ranger residence, Jesse P. Dewitt lived in a tent for eight years. The mining company that owned the site finally agreed in 1916 to rent the Forest Service a parcel for one dollar a year. Civilian Conservation Corps workers later built and improved the station structures. Their camp buildings are gone, but the Forest Service structures they built survive. The Bureau of Land Management acquired the property from the Forest Service in 1970. In 1996, its visitor center received the Smullin name. The former station office now serves as a visitor center.
